cards.grammarNote:
Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and the article shows which:
**le** (masc.) / **la** (fem.); **un** / **une** for 'a'. → **le pain** (bread), **la pomme** (apple). Before a vowel, **le/la → l'**: **l'eau** (water).

cards.english: I am a student. (subject pronoun required)
cards.grammarNote:
French always keeps the subject pronoun, and **être** (to be) is irregular:
**je suis** (I am), **tu es** (you are), **il/elle est** (he/she is), **nous sommes**, **vous êtes**, **ils/elles sont**.

Two words for 'you': **tu** (informal, one person you know) · **vous** (formal, or more than one person):
**tu es** (a friend) vs **vous êtes** (a stranger, or a group). Using **tu** with a stranger can seem too familiar.

cards.english: I don't understand. (ne … pas wraps the verb)
cards.grammarNote:
Negation wraps the verb in two parts: **ne** + verb + **pas**:
**je ne comprends pas** (I don't understand), **je ne sais pas** (I don't know). In casual speech the **ne** is often dropped: **je sais pas**.

**bonjour** = **bon** (good) + **jour** (day), from Latin **bonus dies**.
Used for both 'good morning' and 'good afternoon'. In France, saying bonjour when entering any shop or meeting anyone is culturally essential — skipping it reads as rude.

**s'il vous plaît** = 'if it pleases you' (formal/plural). Informal: **s'il te plaît**.
Breaking it down: **s'il** = si + il (if it) · **vous** = you (formal) · **plaît** = pleases (from **plaire**).
Can open a request: S'il vous plaît, où est… ?

**merci** comes from Latin **mercedem** (payment, reward) — the same root as English 'mercy'.
**Merci beaucoup** = thank you very much · **merci bien** = thanks a lot (can be slightly sarcastic in tone).
Response: **de rien** (you're welcome) or **avec plaisir** (with pleasure, more warm).

**de rien** = literally 'of nothing' — the most common informal response to merci.
More warm alternatives: **avec plaisir** (with pleasure) · **je vous en prie** (formal, 'I beg of you') · **c'est normal** (it's nothing).
In Québec French, **bienvenue** is used for 'you're welcome'.

**bonjour** covers both 'good morning' and 'good afternoon'. **bonsoir** = good evening (from ~6pm). **bonne nuit** = good night (only when going to bed).
In France, saying bonjour when entering a shop is expected.
cards.englishPhrase: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

cards.grammarNote:
**bonne nuit** = **bonne** (good, fem.) + **nuit** (night, fem.) — **la nuit** is feminine.
Only used when someone is going to bed — not as a general evening farewell.
For a daytime farewell: **bonne journée** · evening departure: **bonne soirée**.

Three ways to ask a yes/no question:
1) rising intonation — **Tu parles français ?**  2) add **est-ce que** in front — **Est-ce que tu parles français ?**  3) invert verb + pronoun — **Parles-tu français ?** (most formal).

**comment allez-vous ?** = formal inversion form (**allez-vous** = are you going).
Informal: **comment tu vas ?** or just **ça va ?**
**Comment ça va ?** literally means 'how is it going?' — a very common casual greeting.
The standard reply: **ça va bien, merci** (going well, thanks).
cards.englishPhrase: How are you? Very well, thanks.

cards.grammarNote:
**enchanté(e)** = past participle of **enchanter** (to enchant) — literally 'enchanted'.
Adjectives agree with the speaker's gender: a man says **enchanté**, a woman says **enchantée**.
**Enchanté de faire votre connaissance** is the full, formal phrase.

**au revoir** = **au** (à + le) + **revoir** (to see again) — literally 'until we see each other again'.
Informal: **salut** (also used for hello), **ciao**, **à plus** (see ya), **à tout à l'heure** (see you soon).
**À bientôt** = see you soon · **À demain** = see you tomorrow · **À samedi** = see you Saturday.

**pardon** = excuse me (passing someone or mishearing).
**excusez-moi** = excuse me (getting attention, more formal).
**s'il vous plaît** can also open a request: 'S'il vous plaît, où est…?'
cards.englishPhrase: Excuse me, where is the main street?
cards.phrase: Pardon, où est la rue principale ?

cards.grammarNote:
**désolé** = past participle of **désoler** (to distress), used as an adjective meaning 'sorry'.
Gender agreement: **désolé** (m.) / **désolée** (f.) — a woman says **je suis désolée**.
**Je suis vraiment désolé** = I'm really sorry. **Pardon** is used for smaller apologies or interruptions.

**vouloir** is irregular: je **veux**, tu **veux**, il **veut**, nous **voulons**, vous **voulez**, ils **veulent**.
In a shop or restaurant, **je voudrais** (I would like) is more polite than **je veux** — the conditional softens the request.

**avoir besoin de** = to need (literally 'to have need of').
j'ai besoin d'aide · j'ai besoin de temps
**de** contracts before a vowel: besoin **d'**aide.

**je m'appelle** uses the reflexive verb **s'appeler** — literally 'I call myself'. Much more natural than 'mon nom est'.
The double l in *appelle* preserves the /ɛl/ sound.

**je** becomes **j'** before a vowel or silent h: **j'**aime, **j'**habite, **j'**ai.
This elision is mandatory — *je aime* is never written or spoken.
Subject pronouns in French cannot be dropped as in Spanish; **je** must always appear.

**tu** = informal (one person you know) · **vous** = formal or plural.
Using tu with a stranger can feel rude; vous is always safe. The shift from vous to tu (**tutoyer**) is a social milestone in French relationships.

**il** = he (for a person) or 'it' (for any masculine noun).
**elle** = she, or 'it' for feminine nouns.
Every French noun has grammatical gender — there is no neutral pronoun. **le livre** → il est intéressant. **la table** → elle est grande.

**elle** = she (person) or 'it' for any feminine noun.
Plural: **elles** (all-female group) · **ils** (mixed or all-male group).
Note: a group of 100 women + 1 man = **ils** in traditional grammar — though modern usage is evolving.

**on** is used conversationally to mean 'we' — more common than **nous** in everyday speech.
on takes the same verb form as il/elle: on mange, on va, on est.

**ils** = masculine or mixed-gender group · **elles** = all-feminine group.
Liaison: **ils_** and **elles_** link to a following vowel — **ils_ont**, **elles_arrivent**.
In spoken French, the subject pronoun is always required unlike in languages like Spanish or Italian.

Possessives agree with the thing possessed, not the owner:
**mon** livre (m.) · **ma** table (f.) · **mes** livres (pl.)
Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel: **mon** amie (not *ma amie*).

**ce** (m.) / **cet** (m. before vowel) / **cette** (f.) + noun:
ce livre · cet homme · cette table
As a standalone pronoun: **ceci** (this) · **cela/ça** (that).

French uses the same demonstrative adjectives for 'this' and 'that': **ce/cet/cette/ces**.
To distinguish this vs. that, add **-ci** (here) or **-là** (there): ce livre**-ci** (this book) vs. ce livre**-là** (that book).
**Cette** is feminine: **cette** personne, **cette** table.

French uses **avoir** for hunger, thirst, and temperature — never être:
**j'ai faim** (hungry) · **j'ai soif** (thirsty) · **j'ai froid/chaud** (cold/hot)

**soif** is a feminine noun (la soif) though you rarely see it with an article in this phrase.
**J'ai très soif** — note that **très** modifies the noun here, not an adjective, which is unusual in English ('I'm very thirsty') but natural in French.
Related: **mourir de soif** (dying of thirst — a common hyperbolic expression).

**qui** = who (subject) in both questions and relative clauses.
**Qui est cette personne ?** (question) · **la personne qui parle** (relative clause)
As an object: **que** — **la personne que je connais** (the person I know).

**quoi** = what (standalone or after a preposition): de quoi, avec quoi, pour quoi.
In questions: **qu'est-ce que** (what, as object) is the most common spoken form.
**Que** is used in formal inversion: **Que voulez-vous ?**
Never say *quoi est-ce* — use qu'est-ce que or quoi at the end: Tu veux quoi ?

**quand** = when (question word or conjunction).
As a question: **Quand est-ce que tu arrives ?** or informal **Tu arrives quand ?**
As a conjunction: **quand il pleut** (when it rains) — note that French uses present or future tense after quand for future meaning, just like English.

**où** = where (always with an accent grave to distinguish from the conjunction **ou** = or).
**Où sont les toilettes ?** (formal) · **Les toilettes, c'est où ?** (casual)
Also used in relative clauses: **la ville où j'habite** (the city where I live).

**pourquoi** = **pour** (for) + **quoi** (what) — literally 'for what?'
The answer uses **parce que** (because): **Pourquoi ? Parce que…**
Don't confuse with **car** (for, because) which is more literary.
cards.phrase: Pourquoi tu ne peux pas venir ?

cards.grammarNote:
**comment** = how. Also used for 'what did you say?' (politely): **Comment ?**
**Comment tu vas ?** (informal) · **Comment allez-vous ?** (formal inversion)
**Comment dit-on… ?** = how do you say…? — a useful learner's phrase.

**avoir** is used for physical states (not être):
j'ai faim · j'ai soif · j'ai froid/chaud · j'ai peur
These are 'having' a sensation, not 'being' one.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm hungry. Do you have water?
cards.phrase: J'ai faim. Tu as de l'eau ?

cards.grammarNote:
**faire** = to do AND to make — one verb covers both English meanings.
Irregular: je **fais**, tu **fais**, il **fait**, nous **faisons**, vous **faites**, ils **font**.
Also used for weather: **il fait chaud** (it's hot), **il fait beau** (it's nice out).

**aller + infinitive** = the near future (futur proche):
je vais manger · on va partir · tu vas voir
The most common way to talk about immediate future plans in French.

**venir** is irregular: je **viens**, tu **viens**, il **vient**, nous **venons**, vous **venez**, ils **viennent**.
**venir de + infinitive** = to have just done something (recent past): **je viens de manger** (I just ate).
**Tu viens d'où ?** = Where are you from? — literally 'you come from where?'

**manger** is a regular -er verb but adds an **e** before **-ons** to keep the soft g sound: nous mang**e**ons.
With partitive articles for food: **je mange du pain**, **je mange de la salade**, **je mange des fruits**.
After negation the partitive becomes **de**: je **ne** mange **pas de** viande.

**pouvoir** (to be able to / can) is irregular: je **peux**, tu **peux**, il **peut**, nous **pouvons**, vous **pouvez**, ils **peuvent**.
**Vous pouvez m'aider ?** = informal question (rising intonation)
Formal equivalent: **Pouvez-vous m'aider ?** (inversion).

**voir** is irregular: je **vois**, tu **vois**, il **voit**, nous **voyons**, vous **voyez**, ils **voient**.
**Je ne peux rien voir** — double object: **ne…rien** (nothing) wraps the verb plus infinitive.
**rien** in negation replaces a direct object: je ne vois **rien** (I see nothing) vs. je ne vois **pas** de… (I don't see any…).

**donner** is a regular -er verb.
**Donnez-moi** = give me (imperative + indirect object pronoun **moi**).
Word order with pronouns changes in imperatives: in statements **me** comes before the verb, but in positive imperatives **moi** follows: **donnez-**moi, **donne-**moi.
cards.phrase: Donnez-moi le menu, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**parler** is a regular -er verb: je **parle**, tu **parles**, il **parle**, nous **parlons**, vous **parlez**, ils **parlent**.
Languages follow **parler** directly with no article: **parler français**, **parler anglais** — not *parler le français*.
Note **vous** here — addressing a stranger formally.

**comprendre** (to understand) is conjugated like **prendre**: je **comprends**, tu **comprends**, il **comprend**, nous **comprenons**.
**Je ne comprends pas** — full negation with **ne…pas**.
**Vous comprenez ?** (Do you understand?) uses **vous** for formal/plural address.

**aimer** = to love (people) or to like (things).
**aimer bien** softens it to 'like' rather than 'love': J'aime bien le café. Saying j'aime le café is fine but stronger.

**chercher** = to look for (a regular -er verb: je cherche, tu cherches…).
Importantly, **chercher** already includes 'for' — never say *chercher pour*.
Compare: **trouver** (to find) · **retrouver** (to find again / to meet up with).

**ne…pas** wraps the verb in negation: je **ne** sais **pas**.
In spoken French, **ne** is very commonly dropped: **Je sais pas où c'est.**
**Savoir** (to know a fact) vs. **connaître** (to know a person or place) — two different verbs for 'to know'.
cards.englishPhrase: I don't know where it is.
cards.phrase: Je ne sais pas où c'est.

cards.grammarNote:
**mais** = but. One of the MAISOB conjunctions (mais, alors, if, so, or, but — a classic mnemonic is **MAISOB**: **m**ais, **a**lors, **i**l, **s**i, **o**u, **b**ien).
Note: **mais** vs. **mais non** vs. **mais si** — **mais si** is used to contradict a negative: 'Tu n'aimes pas ça ?' → 'Mais si!' (Yes I do!).
cards.englishPhrase: I want to go, but I can't.
cards.phrase: Je veux y aller, mais je ne peux pas.

cards.grammarNote:
**et** = and. The t is never pronounced before a vowel — no liaison: **et_** + vowel does NOT link.
This is a key exception to liaison rules: 'un café **et** un thé' — the t is silent.
Note the partitive articles in the phrase: **de l'**eau (de + l') and **de la** nourriture.
cards.phrase: De l'eau et de la nourriture.

cards.grammarNote:
**ou** (or) must be distinguished from **où** (where) — the accent marks a completely different word.
**ou bien** = or else / or rather (slightly more emphatic).
In questions: **Thé ou café ?** — rising intonation makes it a question without any question word.

**avec** = with. Preposition, always followed by a noun or pronoun.
**Je suis venu** uses **être** in the passé composé because **venir** is a movement verb — past participle **venu** agrees with the subject (masculine singular here).
A woman would say: **je suis venue** avec mon ami.
cards.phrase: Je suis venu avec mon ami.

cards.grammarNote:
**sans** = without. Always followed by a noun with **no article**: **sans sucre**, **sans lait**, **sans problème**.
With an indefinite article, the article is dropped after **sans**: *café sans un sucre* → **café sans sucre**.
Contrast: **avec** (with) keeps the article: **avec du lait**.
cards.phrase: Café sans sucre, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**pour** = for (purpose, destination, duration in future).
**C'est pour toi** — **toi** is the stressed/disjunctive pronoun (moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles).
Used after prepositions: **pour moi**, **avec toi**, **sans lui**.

**la personne** = person (always feminine, even when referring to a man).
Double duty: **personne** also means 'nobody' in negation: **je ne vois personne** (I see nobody).
Context distinguishes: **une personne** (a person) vs. **ne…personne** (nobody).

**un endroit** = a place, spot, location (masculine).
**un lieu** is a more formal synonym: un lieu de rencontre (a meeting place).
**une place** = a square (public space) or a seat — not a generic 'place': **la place de la Bastille**, **une place dans le train**.
cards.englishPhrase: Do you know a good place?

cards.grammarNote:
**une chose** = a thing (feminine).
**quelque chose** = something (invariable): **tu veux quelque chose ?**
**quelque chose de bon** — after **quelque chose de**, the adjective is always masculine: **quelque chose de délicieux**, **quelque chose d'intéressant**.

**ici** = here (location) · **là** = there, but also used for 'here' in spoken French.
**Viens ici !** = Come here! (using **tu** form of **venir**: viens).
**par ici** = this way · **par là** = that way — useful for giving directions.

**là** = there, but also frequently used to mean 'here' in casual speech: **je suis là** (I'm here).
**là-bas** = over there (more distant) · **là-haut** = up there · **là-dedans** = in there.
Note: **là** (there/here) vs. **la** (the, feminine article) — the accent makes all the difference.

**très** = very (modifies adjectives and some adverbs): **très bien**, **très grand**, **très lentement**.
Don't confuse with **trop** (too/too much): **trop chaud** (too hot) vs. **très chaud** (very hot).
Note: **très** cannot directly modify a noun — use **beaucoup** instead: **beaucoup de travail** (a lot of work).

**eau** is feminine. Use the partitive **de l'eau** for an unspecified amount.
The partitive (**du** / **de la** / **de l'**) is used when quantity is unspecified — very common with food and drink.
cards.phrase: Un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**la nourriture** = food in general (uncountable, feminine).
Alternatives: **les aliments** (foodstuffs, more technical) · **à manger** (something to eat, informal): **j'ai acheté à manger**.
Use the partitive for an unspecified amount: **de la nourriture** (some food).

**la maison** = house or home (feminine). From Latin **mansio**.
**chez moi** = at my place/home — much more natural than 'à ma maison' in everyday speech: **je rentre chez moi** (I'm going home).
**à la maison** = at home (when staying in) · **à la maison** vs. **chez moi** are largely interchangeable.

**le magasin** = store, shop (general).
**une boutique** = a small, often fashionable shop.
**au magasin** — à + le = **au**: je vais **au** magasin.
Specific shops: **la boulangerie** (bakery), **la pharmacie** (pharmacy), **l'épicerie** (grocery).

**les espèces** = cash (always plural in this sense).
**en espèces** = in cash · **par carte** = by card.
Note the formal register of **Vous payez** (are you paying?) — using **vous** to address a customer is standard in shops.
cards.phrase: Vous payez en espèces ou par carte ?

cards.grammarNote:
**l'aide** is feminine: **une aide** (a help/an aid).
**aider** = to help (regular -er verb): **je vous aide ?** (can I help you?)
**Au secours !** = Help! (emergency) · **à l'aide !** = Help! (less urgent, calling for assistance).

**les toilettes** = the toilet/restroom (almost always plural in French).
**la salle de bain** = the bathroom (where you bathe/shower) — the two rooms are often separate in French homes.
In public: **les WC** (pronounced 'veh-say') is also common. Never say **la bathroom** — it's an anglicism.

**toujours** = always OR still (two meanings depending on context).
**Je prends toujours un café** = I always have a coffee.
**Il est toujours là** = He's still there.
**Toujours** comes after the verb in simple tenses and between **avoir/être** and the past participle: **j'ai toujours aimé le café**.
cards.englishPhrase: I always drink coffee in the morning.
cards.phrase: Je prends toujours un café le matin.

cards.grammarNote:
**jamais** pairs with **ne** to form the negative: ne … jamais.
In spoken French the ne is often dropped: J'arrive jamais en retard.
**Jamais** alone in answer to a question means 'never'.

**dans** = inside a space (dans le café) · **sur** = on top of (sur la table)
**en** = in + language/country/material: en français, en France, en coton
**à** = at/to a specific place: à Paris, au magasin
cards.englishPhrase: The book is on the table.
cards.phrase: Le livre est sur la table.

cards.grammarNote:
**de** = from, of, about.
**Je suis de Paris** = I'm from Paris.
**de** contracts with **le** → **du** and with **les** → **des**: **du magasin**, **des enfants**.
Before a vowel: **de l'** — **de l'**école, **de l'**eau.

**bon** (m.) / **bonne** (f.) — agrees with the noun it modifies.
**C'est une bonne idée** — **idée** is feminine, so **bonne**.
**Bien** is also 'good' but as an adverb: **c'est bien** (that's good/nice) vs. **c'est bon** (that tastes good / it's good).

**mauvais** (m.) / **mauvaise** (f.) — adjective agrees with its noun.
**C'est une mauvaise nouvelle** — **nouvelle** (news/a piece of news) is feminine.
Adjective placement: **mauvais** usually precedes the noun: **une mauvaise journée**, **un mauvais signe**.

**grand** (m.) / **grande** (f.) — precedes the noun (BAGS adjective: Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size).
**Un grand café** = a large coffee (or a prestigious café — context matters!).
**Grand** can also mean 'great' or 'tall': **un grand homme** (a great man) vs. **un homme grand** (a tall man). Position changes meaning!
cards.phrase: Un grand café, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**petit** (m.) / **petite** (f.) — precedes the noun, like **grand**.
**Une petite table** — **table** is feminine, so **petite**.
**Petit** also carries affectionate meaning: **mon petit** (my little one/dear). **Petit-déjeuner** = breakfast (literally 'small lunch').
cards.phrase: Une petite table, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**beaucoup** = a lot, much, many.
**beaucoup de** + noun (no article): **beaucoup de travail**, **beaucoup d'eau**, **beaucoup de gens**.
In negation, keep **pas**: **je ne travaille pas beaucoup** (I don't work much).
**Beaucoup** cannot directly modify an adjective — use **très** for that: **très grand**, not *beaucoup grand*.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of work.

cards.grammarNote:
**un peu** = a little. **un peu de** + noun (no article): **un peu d'eau**, **un peu de temps**.
**un peu** can soften adjectives: **c'est un peu difficile** (it's a little difficult).
Contrast: **peu de** (without **un**) = little/not much — more negative in tone: **j'ai peu de temps** (I have little time).
cards.phrase: Un peu d'eau, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**Pouvez-vous** is formal inversion — subject **vous** moves after the verb **pouvez**.
**m'aider** = **me** + **aider** with elision before a vowel: **m'**.
Informal alternative: **Tu peux m'aider ?** (rising intonation, no inversion needed).

**C'est combien ?** = casual, very common.
**Ça coûte combien ?** = more explicit (how much does it cost?).
**Combien ça fait ?** = how much does that come to? (at a till/register).
**Quel est le prix ?** = what is the price? (more formal).

For an unspecified quantity ('some'), French uses the partitive:
**du** (masc.) **du pain** (some bread), **de la** (fem.) **de la viande** (some meat), **de l'** before a vowel **de l'eau**, **des** (plural) **des pommes**.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm eating some bread and some cheese.
cards.phrase: Je mange du pain et du fromage.

cards.english: I would like a coffee. (je voudrais — polite)
cards.grammarNote:
**je voudrais** (I would like) is the polite way to order — softer than **je veux** (I want):
**je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît**. It's the conditional of **vouloir**.
cards.phrase: Je voudrais un thé, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
With **aimer** (to like/love), use the **definite article** for things in general:
**j'aime le café** (I like coffee), **j'aime les pommes** (I like apples). Compare the partitive **du café** = 'some coffee' (a quantity).

**l'eau** is feminine. Use the partitive **de l'eau** for an unspecified amount: Je bois de l'eau.
A definite quantity uses un verre d'eau, une bouteille d'eau, etc.
The partitive (**du** / **de la** / **de l'**) is essential with food and drink.

**le pain** is masculine. Use the partitive **du pain** for an unspecified amount: **Je voudrais du pain**.
After negation the partitive becomes **de**: **je ne mange pas de pain**.
French bread culture: **une baguette**, **un pain de campagne** (country loaf), **une ficelle** (thin baguette).

**le riz** is masculine. The z is silent in **le riz** but can be heard in liaison before a vowel: **du riz_au lait** (rice pudding).
Partitive: **du riz** (some rice) — not *un riz* because rice is uncountable.
Adjective agreement: **des légumes** (plural) — the verb **aimer** with a definite article means a general preference.
cards.phrase: J'aime le riz avec des légumes.

cards.grammarNote:
**le lait** is masculine (from Latin **lac/lactis**, root of English 'lactose').
Partitive: **du lait** — **Tu veux du lait ?** asks 'do you want some milk?'
After negation: **je ne veux pas de lait** (no article after **de** in negation).

Singular: **l'œuf** — the f is pronounced.
Plural: **les œufs** — the f goes silent! Pronounced 'leh-ZUH'. A classic French pronunciation trap.
cards.englishPhrase: I eat two eggs for breakfast.
cards.phrase: Je mange deux œufs au petit-déjeuner.

cards.grammarNote:
**le fromage** is masculine. Use partitive **du fromage** for an unspecified quantity.
France has over 1,000 cheese varieties — **le fromage** is culturally significant.
**a du fromage** in the example — this is the partitive, meaning the sandwich contains some cheese (not a whole cheese).

**le poulet** = chicken (as food). As a live animal: **la poule** (hen) or **le coq** (rooster).
Definite article **le** here: **le poulet est délicieux** — a general statement about this chicken.
Partitive for unspecified amount: **Je mange du poulet** (I'm eating [some] chicken).

**la viande** is feminine. Partitive would be **de la viande**.
Negation changes partitive to **de**: **il ne mange pas de viande** — the article drops after **ne…pas**.
This rule applies to all partitives and indefinite articles in negation: **du pain** → **pas de pain**, **une pomme** → **pas de pomme**.
cards.phrase: Il ne mange pas de viande.

cards.grammarNote:
**le poisson** = fish (food or animal). **la poissonnerie** = fishmonger's shop.
**J'aime le poisson** — the definite article **le** with **aimer** expresses a general preference, not a specific fish.
Nasal vowel: **poisson** contains the nasal **on** — pronounced like the end of 'song' in English.

**le fruit** (singular) / **les fruits** (plural). **Des fruits** = the partitive/indefinite plural for some fruit.
**Tous les jours** = every day — **tous** (m. pl.) agrees with **les jours** (m. pl.). Compare: **toutes les semaines** (f. pl.).
In English 'fruit' is typically uncountable; in French, individual fruits are counted: **un fruit**, **deux fruits**.
cards.phrase: Je mange des fruits tous les jours.

cards.grammarNote:
**la pomme** is feminine. Literally means 'apple' but appears in: **la pomme de terre** (potato — lit. 'apple of the earth') and **la pomme d'Adam** (Adam's apple).
**par jour** = per day — **par** is used for rates and frequencies.
**la santé** = health (feminine). The phrase **c'est bon pour la santé** is very commonly used.
cards.englishPhrase: An apple a day is healthy.
cards.phrase: Une pomme par jour, c'est bon pour la santé.

cards.grammarNote:
**le café** = coffee (the drink) AND the café (the establishment).
**le matin** = in the morning (definite article with time expressions for habitual action: **le soir**, **le week-end**).
**J'aime le café** — definite article **le** with **aimer** = general preference (I like coffee in general).
cards.englishPhrase: I like coffee in the morning.

cards.grammarNote:
**le thé** is masculine. The accent aigu (é) indicates the /e/ vowel sound.
**du thé** — partitive article: **Tu veux du thé ?** = would you like some tea?
Tea is less embedded in French daily culture than coffee — **un thé** is typically offered after dinner or for medicinal purposes.

**le vin** is masculine. Nasal vowel: **in** — the n is not pronounced, the vowel is nasalised.
**un verre de vin rouge** — a countable serving (un verre = one glass). No partitive here because 'a glass of' specifies the quantity.
Types: **le vin rouge** (red), **le vin blanc** (white), **le vin rosé** (rosé).
cards.englishPhrase: A glass of red wine, please.
cards.phrase: Un verre de vin rouge, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**la bière** is feminine. The grave accent on **è** signals the open /ɛ/ sound.
**Deux bières** — indefinite plural for two specific beers (countable order).
In a café: **une pression** = a draught beer (pint) · **une bouteille** = a bottled beer.

**le sucre** is masculine. **sans sucre** — the preposition **sans** (without) always drops the article: **sans sucre**, **sans lait**, **sans gluten**.
In a café or restaurant, 'un sucre' can mean one sugar cube: **un café avec un sucre**.

**le sel** is masculine. From Latin **sal** — root of 'salary' (Roman soldiers were sometimes paid in salt).
**Tu peux me passer le sel ?** — indirect object pronoun **me** (to me) before the verb: **me passer**.
This is a polite way to ask — more direct: **Passe-moi le sel !** (imperative).
cards.phrase: Tu peux me passer le sel ?

cards.grammarNote:
**manger** is a regular -er verb with a spelling change: **nous mangeons** (adds **e** to keep the soft g sound before **-ons**).
**On mange !** = Let's eat! — **on** used for 'we' in casual French, takes the same verb form as **il/elle**.
With partitives: **je mange du pain**, **de la salade**, **des légumes** (some bread/salad/vegetables).

**boire** is irregular: je **bois**, tu **bois**, il **boit**, nous **buvons**, vous **buvez**, ils **boivent**.
**quelque chose à boire** = something to drink — **à + infinitive** expresses purpose after **quelque chose**.
With partitives: **boire du vin**, **boire de la bière**, **boire de l'eau**.
cards.englishPhrase: Would you like something to drink?
cards.phrase: Tu veux quelque chose à boire ?

cards.grammarNote:
French uses **avoir** for hunger, thirst, and physical sensations — never être:
**avoir faim** (hungry) · **avoir soif** (thirsty) · **avoir froid/chaud** (cold/hot) · **avoir peur** (afraid)

**soif** (thirst) is feminine — **la soif**. In the expression **avoir soif** it appears without an article.
**Tu as soif ?** — informal question by rising intonation; no inversion needed.
Related: **mourir de soif** (to be dying of thirst) — a very common hyperbolic expression in French.

**le petit-déjeuner** = breakfast, literally 'the little lunch'.
**prendre le petit-déjeuner** = to have breakfast — meals are 'taken' (**prendre**) in French, not 'eaten' or 'had'.
**à sept heures** — time with **à**: note no contraction since **heures** is feminine (à + la = à la, but **heures** doesn't need an article here).
cards.phrase: Je prends le petit-déjeuner à sept heures.

cards.grammarNote:
**le déjeuner** = lunch (also the verb **déjeuner** = to have lunch).
**On déjeune** — here **déjeuner** is used as a verb, not a noun. Same word does double duty.
**à deux heures** — France typically lunches between 12h and 14h; 'two o'clock' is late but not unusual on weekends.

**le dîner** = dinner/evening meal (also the verb **dîner** = to dine).
The circumflex on **î** reflects a historical **s**: Old French **disner**.
**Le dîner est prêt** — adjective **prêt** (ready, m.) agrees with **le dîner** (m.). Feminine: **la soupe est prête**.

**la baguette** is feminine — literally 'a little rod/wand' (same word used for a conductor's baton and magic wand).
**Je voudrais** = I would like — the conditional of **vouloir**, used for polite requests.
**une baguette** uses the indefinite article (one specific baguette), not the partitive.
cards.phrase: Je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**le croissant** = crescent (its shape). From French **croître** (to grow), related to the crescent moon shape.
**Je prends** (I'm having/taking) is a common way to order at a café — more casual than **je voudrais**.
**au beurre** = with butter — **au** is **à + le** (contraction). A **croissant au beurre** is made with real butter (richer and flakier than a plain croissant).
cards.phrase: Je prends un croissant au beurre.

cards.grammarNote:
**la crêpe** is feminine. The circumflex on the **ê** indicates a historical 's' (Old French: **crespe**) — compare English 'crisp'.
**au chocolat** = with chocolate — **au** is **à + le** (**le chocolat** is masculine).
**Je veux** here is direct — in a casual context acceptable. For a shop, **je voudrais** is more polite.
cards.phrase: Je veux une crêpe au chocolat.

cards.grammarNote:
**le porc** = pork (food). The c is silent: pronounced 'por'.
Negation: **je ne mange pas de porc** — the partitive **du** drops to **de** after **ne…pas**.
Animal: **le cochon** or **le porc** — in English 'pig' and 'pork' differ (Germanic vs. Latin roots); French uses **le porc** for both.
cards.phrase: Je ne mange pas de porc.

cards.grammarNote:
**la banane** is feminine. An easy gender rule: most nouns ending in **-ane** are feminine.
**Les bananes sont mûres** — adjective **mûr** agrees with the feminine plural noun: **mûres**.
In French slang, **une banane** can mean a big grin (un grand sourire en forme de banane).

**l'orange** is feminine — unusual because words ending in a consonant sound are often masculine.
**jus d'orange** — note no article after **de** when combining nouns: **jus de** + orange (not *jus de l'orange*).
**Je veux un jus d'orange** — here **un jus** = one glass/serving of juice (countable).

**le légume** is masculine (despite the feminine-looking **-e** ending).
**Mange tes légumes !** — imperative of **manger** (tu form: **mange**) + possessive **tes** (your, plural object).
**Tes** = plural of **ton/ta** — used because **légumes** is plural.

**la pomme de terre** = potato, literally 'apple of the earth'. Always feminine.
Plural: **les pommes de terre** — the whole compound pluralises.
**de la purée** — partitive article for the mashed potato (uncountable quantity).
cards.phrase: Je veux de la purée de pommes de terre.

cards.grammarNote:
**la tomate** is feminine (ending in **-ate**, a common feminine pattern).
**des tomates** — partitive/indefinite plural: the salad has some tomatoes (unspecified quantity).
**a des tomates** — **avoir** + partitive for 'has/contains some': the salad has [some] tomatoes.

**l'oignon** is masculine. The spelling is irregular — the **oi** is not pronounced as usual; it sounds like 'on-yon'.
Negation: **je n'aime pas les oignons** — **ne** elides to **n'** before a vowel.
**les oignons** — definite article **les** with **aimer** expresses general dislike.

**la salade** is feminine. Can mean the salad dish OR the lettuce plant itself.
**Je vais prendre** = I'm going to have — **aller + infinitive** is the near future (futur proche).
**une salade** — indefinite article because it's a specific order (one salad), not a partitive.

**la soupe** is feminine. From Old French **soupe** (bread soaked in broth) — same root as 'supper'.
Adjective agreement: **chaude** is the feminine form of **chaud** (hot), agreeing with **la soupe**.
Partitive for serving: **de la soupe** (some soup) — useful when asking for or offering.

**le sandwich** is masculine (borrowed English word, keeps the masculine gender by default for foreign borrowings in French).
**j'ai fait** = passé composé of **faire** (to make/do): **avoir** + past participle **fait**.
**pour le déjeuner** — meals take the definite article: **le déjeuner**, **le dîner**, **le petit-déjeuner**.
cards.englishPhrase: I made a sandwich for lunch.
cards.phrase: J'ai fait un sandwich pour le déjeuner.

cards.grammarNote:
**le jus** is masculine. The s is silent in isolation but heard in liaison: **le jus_orange** (no liaison needed here since it's **jus d'orange**).
**du jus d'orange** — partitive **du** (de + le) for an unspecified quantity of juice.
**jus de** + fruit name: **jus de pomme** (apple juice), **jus d'orange** (orange juice).

**cuisiner** = to cook (general). **faire la cuisine** is an equivalent common expression.
**Elle cuisine très bien** — adverb **bien** (well) modifies the verb directly.
**Le cuisinier / la cuisinière** = the cook (person). **La cuisinière** also means the stove — same word, two meanings.

**le repas** = meal (masculine). Plural: **les repas** — the s is already there, so the plural looks identical in writing.
**un repas délicieux** — adjective follows the noun here (most adjectives do in French).
The traditional French meal is sacred — **le repas** often refers to the structured, multi-course event.

**la carte** = the full menu (order anything you like).
**le menu** in France = a set-price meal: entrée + plat + dessert.
Always ask for la carte to order freely.

**le restaurant** is masculine. From **restaurer** (to restore) — originally a restorative broth sold in Paris in the 18th century.
**Ce restaurant** — demonstrative adjective **ce** (this/that, masculine singular).
**est bien** vs. **est bon** — **bien** here means 'good' in quality/service; **bon** would imply good taste.

**le serveur** = waiter (m.) / **la serveuse** = waitress (f.).
To get a waiter's attention: **Monsieur !** (not 'garçon' — that is now considered rude).
**l'addition** = the bill (la addition → l'addition). In a café: **l'addition, s'il vous plaît** or just **vous pouvez nous apporter l'addition ?**

**la table** is feminine (from Latin **tabula**, feminine).
**Notre table** = our table — **notre** is the possessive adjective for 'our' (same form for m. and f. singular).
**est prête** — adjective **prêt** agrees with the feminine noun **la table**: **prête**.

**l'assiette** is feminine. From Old French **asseoir** (to sit/set) — a plate is something that is 'set'.
**sale** = dirty (adjective following the noun via **être**). Before a noun **sale** also means dirty: **une sale affaire** (a dirty business).
**l'assiette** — the l' before a vowel is elision of **le** or **la** (can't tell gender from this form alone — but it's feminine).

**le verre** = a glass (drinking vessel) AND the material 'glass'. Masculine.
**un verre d'eau** — the **de** after a container word drops the article: un verre **de** vin, une tasse **de** café, une bouteille **d'**eau.
cards.phrase: Un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**la bouteille** is feminine. The **-eille** ending is always feminine: **la bouteille**, **la corbeille**, **la groseille**.
**une bouteille de vin** — container + **de** + noun (no article): **une bouteille de vin**, **un verre d'eau**, **une tasse de café**.
cards.phrase: Une bouteille de vin, s'il vous plaît.

cards.grammarNote:
**le gâteau** is masculine. Plural: **les gâteaux** (the x replaces s in the plural — a pattern for words ending in **-eau**: bateau → bateaux, chapeau → chapeaux).
**du gâteau** — partitive: do you want some cake? (unspecified amount, not a whole cake).

**le biscuit** = biscuit/cookie. From Latin **bis coctus** (twice cooked) — same etymology as English 'biscuit'.
**ces biscuits** — demonstrative adjective **ces** (these/those, plural) agrees with the masculine plural noun.
**sont délicieux** — adjective **délicieux** is masculine plural, agreeing with **les biscuits**.

**le chocolat** is masculine. From Nahuatl **xocolātl** via Spanish.
**J'adore** = I love (stronger than **j'aime**) — no partitive needed with **adorer/aimer** + definite article for general statements.
**le chocolat** here = chocolate in general (definite article for category love).

**le beurre** is masculine. From Latin **butyrum**, from Greek **βούτυρον**.
**du beurre** — partitive article: I put some butter (unspecified amount) on my bread.
**sur mon pain** — possessive **mon** (my, masculine) + **pain** (m.). **mets** = present tense of **mettre** (to put), an irregular verb.
cards.englishPhrase: I put butter on my bread.
cards.phrase: Je mets du beurre sur mon pain.

cards.grammarNote:
**l'huile** is feminine — the h is aspirate so liaison/elision applies: **de l'huile**, not *de la huile*.
**de l'huile d'olive** — partitive (de + l') then a noun+de+noun compound without article.
**Cuisinez** = the vous imperative of **cuisiner** (to cook, a regular -er verb).

**le poivre** = pepper (the spice, masculine). **le poivron** = bell pepper (a different word).
**Tu peux me passer** — same indirect object pronoun structure as with **le sel**.
Note: in French cooking, **sel et poivre** (salt and pepper) is the standard order, same as English.
cards.phrase: Tu peux me passer le poivre ?

cards.grammarNote:
**la cuisine** = the kitchen (room) AND cooking/cuisine.
**La cuisine française** = French cuisine (cooking). **la cuisine** (room in the house).
**propre** = clean. Note: **propre** before a noun means 'own' (**ma propre voiture** = my own car), but after être it means 'clean'.

**le four** is masculine. From Latin **furnus** — also the root of **la fournée** (a batch of baked goods).
**au four** = in the oven — **à + le = au**: **faire cuire au four** (to bake/roast in the oven).
Adjective agreement: **chaud** (hot, masculine) agrees with **le four** (m.).

**la cuisinière** = the stove/cooker (feminine). Also means 'female cook'.
**Faites-le cuire** = imperative of **faire** (vous form) + direct object pronoun **le** before the infinitive **cuire**.
**sur les plaques** = on the burners/hobs — **les plaques** (f. pl.) means hobs/rings on a cooktop.

**le couteau** is masculine. Plural: **les couteaux** (x replaces s, like **gâteaux**).
**bien aiguisé** = well-sharpened — **bien** modifies the past participle **aiguisé** (used as adjective).
**avoir besoin d'un** — **de + un = d'un** (elision before vowel in **un**).
cards.phrase: J'ai besoin d'un couteau bien aiguisé.

cards.grammarNote:
**la fourchette** is feminine. Diminutive of **la fourche** (pitchfork) — a small fork.
The **-ette** suffix is always feminine: **la fourchette**, **la baguette**, **la serviette**.
**Je peux avoir** = can I have — **pouvoir + infinitive** (informal question by rising intonation, no inversion).

**la cuillère** is feminine. Also spelled **cuiller** (an older form).
**une cuillère à café** = a teaspoon (literally 'a coffee spoon') · **une cuillère à soupe** = a tablespoon.
**j'ai besoin d'une** — elision: **de + une** becomes **d'une** before vowel.

French has no single verb equivalent to 'bake' — it uses **faire cuire au four** (to cook in the oven).
**du pain** — partitive article: I bake some bread (unspecified amount).
**le dimanche** — definite article with days of the week for habitual actions: **le lundi** (every Monday), **le dimanche** (every Sunday). No article = a specific day: **dimanche** (this Sunday).
cards.phrase: Je fais cuire du pain au four le dimanche.

cards.grammarNote:
**frire** (to deep fry) is defective — it has limited forms and is rarely used in everyday speech.
**Faire revenir** is the preferred expression for sautéing onions in oil: **faites revenir** (vous imperative).
**dans l'huile** — preposition **dans** (in/into) for the medium you're cooking in.
cards.phrase: Faites revenir les oignons dans l'huile.

cards.grammarNote:
**mélanger** = to mix. Like **manger**, it adds **e** before **-ons**: **nous mélangeons**.
**Mélangez** = vous imperative.
**tous les ingrédients** — **tous** (all, masculine plural) + **les ingrédients**. Pronounced 'tooss': the s is pronounced before a vowel in **tous** when it's a pronoun, but silent when it's an adjective.

**verser** = to pour. A regular -er verb.
**Versez l'eau** — direct object **l'eau** (definite article — the specific water you have).
**dans le verre** — **dans** (into/in) for pouring into a container. Compare: **sur** (onto): **versez sur le gâteau**.
cards.englishPhrase: Pour the water into the glass.

cards.grammarNote:
**servir** = to serve. Irregular -ir verb: je **sers**, tu **sers**, il **sert**, nous **servons**.
**a servi** = passé composé with **avoir**: **avoir** + past participle **servi**.
**le serveur** (waiter) comes from **servir** — the person who serves.
cards.phrase: Le serveur a servi la nourriture.

cards.grammarNote:
**frais** (m.) / **fraîche** (f.) — an irregular feminine form.
**Le pain est frais** — adjective after **être** agrees with subject: **le pain** (m.) → **frais**.
For a woman or feminine noun: **la crème est fraîche**. **Frais** also means 'cool' in weather: **il fait frais** (it's cool/fresh outside).

**cuit** = past participle of **cuire** (to cook), used as an adjective meaning 'cooked'.
**Le poulet est cuit ?** — **cuit** is masculine, agreeing with **le poulet**. Feminine: **la viande est cuite**.
Degrees of doneness: **bien cuit** (well-done), **à point** (medium), **saignant** (rare — literally 'bleeding').

**chaud** (m.) / **chaude** (f.) — adjective agrees with its noun.
**La soupe est chaude** — feminine agreement with **la soupe**.
For people and sensations use **avoir**: **j'ai chaud** (I'm hot), not *je suis chaud* (which has slang meanings to avoid).
cards.englishPhrase: Be careful, the soup is hot.

cards.grammarNote:
**froid** (m.) / **froide** (f.) — adjective agrees with its noun.
**Mon café est froid** — **froid** is masculine, agreeing with **le café** (m.).
For body temperature use **avoir**: **j'ai froid** (I'm cold). For weather: **il fait froid** (it's cold). Never *je suis froid* for temperature.

**sucré** = sweet (literally 'sugared') — past participle of **sucrer** used as adjective.
**Ce gâteau est très sucré** — **sucré** is masculine, agreeing with **le gâteau** (m.).
Contrast: **le sucre** (the noun, sugar) vs. **sucré** (the adjective, sweet/sugary). **Un dessert sucré** = a sweet dessert.

**épicé** (m.) / **épicée** (f.) — past participle of **épicer** (to spice) used as an adjective.
**La cuisine mexicaine est souvent épicée** — feminine agreement: **cuisine** (f.) → **épicée**.
**souvent** (often) = adverb modifying the verb/adjective. Note **-tion** words like **la cuisine** are not **-tion** words — but all **-tion** nouns are feminine in French.
cards.phrase: La cuisine mexicaine est souvent épicée.

cards.grammarNote:
**c'est** (it is / that is) + adjective gives a quick reaction:
**c'est délicieux** (it's delicious), **c'est bon** (it's good). The adjective stays masculine singular after **c'est**.

**délicieux** (m.) / **délicieuse** (f.) — adjectives ending in **-eux** change to **-euse** in the feminine.
**C'est délicieux !** — **c'est** + adjective: when commenting on something without naming it, use the invariable **c'est** + masculine adjective.
For a named feminine noun: **cette tarte est délicieuse**.

**sain** (m.) / **saine** (f.) = healthy.
The example uses **bons pour la santé** (good for health) — a very common alternative to **sains**.
**la santé** = health (feminine). **Être en bonne santé** = to be in good health. **À votre santé !** = Cheers! (literally 'to your health!').
cards.phrase: Les fruits sont bons pour la santé.

cards.grammarNote:
**végétarien** (m.) / **végétarienne** (f.) — double n in the feminine form.
**Je suis végétarien(ne)** — with **être**, nationality/religion/profession adjectives have no article.
Compare: **je suis médecin** (I'm a doctor) — no article before profession after **être**.

cards.english: There is a bank. (il y a)
cards.grammarNote:
**il y a** = there is / there are — one fixed phrase for both:
**il y a une banque** (there's a bank), **il y a deux musées** (there are two museums). Literally 'it there has'.
cards.phrase: Il y a un restaurant près d'ici ?

cards.grammarNote:
Common position words:
**dans** (in) **dans la maison**, **sur** (on) **sur la table**, **sous** (under) **sous le lit**, **devant** (in front of), **derrière** (behind), **à côté de** (next to).
cards.englishPhrase: The cat is on the table.
cards.phrase: Le chat est sur la table.

cards.grammarNote:
**à** and **de** contract before masculine **le** and plural **les**:
**à + le → au**, **à + les → aux**; **de + le → du**, **de + les → des**. → **au parc** (to the park), **la porte du café**. No change with **la** or **l'**.

**Je rentre** = I'm going back home (implies returning). **Je vais** à la maison is also correct but less natural.
**chez moi** is the more colloquial alternative: je rentre chez moi (I'm going home / back to my place).

**l'appartement** starts with a vowel, so the definite article elides: **l'**appartement.
**dans un appartement** uses **dans** (in, inside) — not **à** — because you are physically inside a space rather than just located at a place.

**aller à + l'école** — no contraction needed before a vowel: **à l'école** (not *à la école*).
**vont** is the third-person plural of **aller**: je vais · tu vas · il va · nous allons · vous allez · ils **vont**.

**à l'université** — **à** + vowel-initial noun: no contraction, just elision of the article to **l'**.
**étudier** is a regular **-er** verb: j'étudie · tu étudies · il/elle étudie.

**dans un bureau** uses **dans** (inside a space).
**Le bureau** also means 'desk' — context makes the meaning clear: il est au bureau (he's at the office) vs. il est sur le bureau (it's on the desk).

**à + le = au** · **à + les = aux** · **de + le = du** — these contractions are mandatory.
Before vowels, **l'** already elides: à l'hôpital, de l'hôpital — no further contraction needed.

**au supermarché** — **à + le = au** (mandatory contraction).
**avoir besoin de + infinitive** = to need to do something: j'ai besoin **d'**aller (before a vowel, **de** elides to **d'**).
cards.englishPhrase: I need to go to the supermarket.

cards.grammarNote:
**venir de + place** = to come from a place: je viens **de la** banque · je viens **du** marché · je viens **de l'**hôpital.
**de + le = du** · **de + la = de la** (no contraction for feminine) · **de + les = des**.

**à la bibliothèque** — feminine noun, so **à la** (no contraction).
Note: **la bibliothèque** = library (borrowing books); **la librairie** = bookshop (buying books) — a common false friend for English speakers.

**complet** here means 'full / no tables available', not 'complete'.
To say you're going to the restaurant: **je vais au restaurant** — **à + le = au** (mandatory contraction).

**au café** — **à + le = au** (mandatory contraction).
**se retrouver** = to meet up (by arrangement): on se retrouve au café. This is a reflexive verb: je me retrouve · tu te retrouves · on se retrouve.

**en centre-ville** uses **en** without an article — a fixed expression for 'downtown/in the city centre'.
**l'hôtel** — the H is aspirate in **hôtel**, so no liaison: *les hôtels* is pronounced without the S sound of **les** linking to **hôtel**.

**loin d'ici** — **de + ici** contracts to **d'ici** (before a vowel).
To say 'I'm going to the airport': **je vais à l'aéroport** — no contraction needed because the noun starts with a vowel.
cards.englishPhrase: The airport is far from here.

cards.grammarNote:
**près de + l'hôtel** = near the hotel. Before a vowel, **de** elides: **de l'hôtel**.
**La gare** = train station; **la station** = metro/bus stop or ski resort; **l'aéroport** = airport.
cards.englishPhrase: The station is near the hotel.
cards.phrase: La gare est près de l'hôtel.

cards.grammarNote:
**à l'arrêt de bus** — **à + l'** before a vowel (no contraction needed, just elision).
**Attends** is the **tu** imperative of **attendre** (to wait). Regular -re imperative: drop the **-s** of the tu form — tu attends → attends !

cards.english: I'm going to the park. (aller à + place)
cards.grammarNote:
**aller** (to go) + **à** for a destination; **à + le → au**:
**je vais au parc**, **je vais à la plage** (to the beach). **aller** is irregular: **je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont**.

**dans le parc** uses **dans** (physically inside the park space).
**jouer** is a regular **-er** verb: je joue · tu joues · ils jouent. Note the silent final **-ent** of the third-person plural.
cards.englishPhrase: The children play in the park.
cards.phrase: Les enfants jouent dans le parc.

cards.grammarNote:
**il y a** = there is / there are. The **y** is a location pronoun meaning 'there'; **il y a** is a fixed expression.
**une pharmacie** — feminine noun: **une** (indefinite article fem.).
**près d'ici** — **de + ici** contracts to **d'ici** before a vowel.
cards.phrase: Est-ce qu'il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?

cards.grammarNote:
**dans cette rue** — **dans** (in/along this street). **Cette** is the demonstrative adjective feminine singular: ce (masc.) · cette (fem.) · ces (plural).
**La rue** vs. **l'avenue** vs. **le boulevard** — all types of streets, but different in French address conventions.
cards.englishPhrase: The restaurant is on this street.
cards.phrase: Le restaurant est dans cette rue.

cards.grammarNote:
**on a traversé** — **on** is widely used in informal French to mean 'we'. Here it uses **avoir** in the passé composé: **on a** + past participle.
**traverser** = to cross (a bridge, a street, a city). Past participle: traversé (regular -er verb).

**au coin** — **à + le = au** (mandatory contraction).
**Tournez à droite au coin** — compare **au coin de la rue** (at the street corner) for more specific directions.

**en centre-ville** — fixed expression using **en** without an article (like **en ville** = in town).
**Le musée est en centre-ville** vs. **je vais au centre-ville** — use **en** for location, **au** (à + le) when going there.

**dans un quartier calme** — **dans** for being inside an area/zone.
**Calme** is an adjective that stays the same for masculine and feminine: un quartier **calme** · une rue **calme**.
cards.englishPhrase: I live in a quiet neighbourhood.

cards.grammarNote:
**La plage est belle** — adjective **belle** is the feminine form of **beau**: un beau paysage · une belle plage.
To go to the beach: **aller à la plage** (feminine noun, so no contraction).

**très haute** — **haute** is the feminine form of **haut** (high/tall). Adjective agreement: **haut** (masc.) · **haute** (fem.).
Location: **en montagne** (in the mountains — no article, fixed expression) vs. **dans la montagne** (in/through the mountain).

**je veux visiter** — **vouloir + infinitive** = to want to do something. Present tense: je veux · tu veux · il veut · nous voulons · vous voulez · ils veulent.
**Le musée** — masculine noun ending in **-ée** (unusual; most nouns in **-ée** are feminine).
cards.englishPhrase: I want to visit the museum.

cards.grammarNote:
**au cinéma** — **à + le = au** (mandatory contraction).
**on va** — **on** used colloquially for 'we'. **Aller + infinitive** (futur proche) = near future: on va au cinéma (we're going to the cinema).
cards.englishPhrase: We're going to the cinema tonight.
cards.phrase: On va au cinéma ce soir.

cards.grammarNote:
Note: **un plan** = a street map (of a city); **une carte** = a map (geographic, playing card, or menu).
Here, **vous avez un plan ?** uses inversion-free question form — natural in spoken French.

**Dans quelle direction** — **dans** is used with **direction** (not **en** or **à**): dans quelle direction est la gare ?
**Quelle** is the interrogative adjective feminine: **quel** (masc.) · **quelle** (fem.).
cards.phrase: Dans quelle direction est la gare ?

cards.grammarNote:
**dans le sac** — **dans** = inside (a container, space, or bounded area).
Do not confuse with **en** (mode/state) or **à** (location at a point). Compare: je suis **dans** la voiture (in the car) vs. je suis **en** voiture (travelling by car).
cards.englishPhrase: The keys are in the bag.
cards.phrase: Les clés sont dans le sac.

cards.grammarNote:
**sur la table** — **sur** = on top of / on a surface.
Contrast: **sous la table** (under the table) · **dans le tiroir** (in the drawer) · **à côté de la table** (next to the table).
cards.englishPhrase: The book is on the table.
cards.phrase: Le livre est sur la table.

cards.grammarNote:
**au bureau** — **à + le = au** (mandatory contraction).
**à** expresses location at a specific point: **à** la maison, **au** bureau, **à** l'école.
Also used for times: **à** cinq heures, and cities: **à** Paris, **à** Londres.

**sous la table** — **sous** = under/beneath.
**sous** never contracts like **à** or **de**. Contrast: **sur** (on) · **sous** (under) · **dans** (in) · **devant** (in front of) · **derrière** (behind).
cards.englishPhrase: The cat is under the table.
cards.phrase: Le chat est sous la table.

cards.grammarNote:
**à côté du café** — **à côté de + le = à côté du** (**de + le = du** — mandatory contraction).
**à côté de** is a compound preposition and always requires **de**: à côté **de** la banque · à côté **du** parc.
cards.englishPhrase: The bank is next to the cafe.
cards.phrase: La banque est à côté du café.

cards.grammarNote:
**entre** does not contract: entre **l'**école et **la** bibliothèque.
**entre A et B** = between A and B — same structure as English. **Entre** is also used idiomatically: entre nous (between us/between you and me).
cards.englishPhrase: The park is between the school and the library.
cards.phrase: Le parc est entre l'école et la bibliothèque.

cards.grammarNote:
**devant l'hôtel** — **devant** = in front of / outside (facing). It does not contract.
**devant** vs. **face à**: **devant** indicates physical position in front; **face à** can be more figurative (facing a challenge).
cards.englishPhrase: The taxi is in front of the hotel.

cards.grammarNote:
**derrière la maison** — **derrière** = behind. It does not contract.
**derrière** (behind) is the spatial opposite of **devant** (in front of). Also used figuratively: derrière cette décision (behind this decision).
cards.englishPhrase: The garden is behind the house.
cards.phrase: Le jardin est derrière la maison.

cards.grammarNote:
**près d'ici** — **près de + ici**: **de** elides to **d'** before a vowel.
**près de** always requires **de**: près **de** la gare · près **du** parc (**de + le = du**) · près **de l'**hôpital.
cards.englishPhrase: Is there a restaurant near here?
cards.phrase: Il y a un restaurant près d'ici ?

cards.grammarNote:
**loin** without **de** when used alone (no following noun): l'aéroport est **loin**.
With a noun: **loin de** la gare · **loin du** centre-ville (**de + le = du**).
**loin** is the opposite of **près** (near).

**ici** = here (a fixed location). **là** = there (or 'here' in informal speech).
**Viens** is the **tu** imperative of **venir** (irregular): viens ! · venez ! (vous form).

**là-bas** = over there (a more distant location). **là** alone = there/here (nearby).
**là-bas** adds **-bas** (lit. down-there) to indicate something further away. Compare: il est **là** (he's here/right there) vs. il est **là-bas** (he's over there).

**à gauche** = to the left / on the left. Always used with **à**: tournez **à** gauche.
**la gauche** (with article) = the left (politically or directionally): à **ma** gauche = to my left.

**à droite** = to the right / on the right. Always used with **à**: tournez **à** droite.
**droite** and **gauche** are feminine nouns when used as directions: **la** droite · **la** gauche.

**tout droit** is an adverbial phrase that never changes form (no agreement).
**Allez tout droit** — **allez** is the **vous** imperative of **aller** (irregular). Contrast **à droite** (to the right) — the word **droit** means 'straight' as an adverb, but **droite** (feminine noun) means 'the right direction'.

**au nord** — **à + le = au**. Cardinal directions use the masculine definite article: **le** nord · **le** sud · **l'**est · **l'**ouest.
Location: **au nord de Paris** = north of Paris · **dans le nord** = in the north (of France).
cards.englishPhrase: The city is to the north.

cards.grammarNote:
**au sud** — **à + le = au**. Same pattern as all cardinal directions.
**le sud de la France** = the south of France. Note: **le Midi** is also used colloquially for the south of France.
cards.englishPhrase: The beach is to the south.

cards.grammarNote:
**à l'est** — **l'est** starts with a vowel, so no contraction after **à**.
**se lever** = to rise (reflexive): le soleil **se lève** — third-person singular reflexive. Also the verb for 'to get up': je me lève à sept heures.
cards.englishPhrase: The sun rises in the east.
cards.phrase: Le soleil se lève à l'est.

cards.grammarNote:
**à l'ouest** — vowel-initial, so **à l'** (no contraction needed).
**se coucher** = to set (of the sun) / to go to bed (reflexive): le soleil **se couche** · je me couche à dix heures.
cards.englishPhrase: The sun sets in the west.
cards.phrase: Le soleil se couche à l'ouest.

cards.grammarNote:
**à proximité** = nearby (formal/written); **près d'ici** = nearby (conversational).
**une pharmacie à proximité** — **à proximité** follows the noun it modifies, unlike English 'nearby pharmacy' where the adjective precedes.
cards.phrase: Il y a une pharmacie à proximité ?

cards.grammarNote:
**aller** is highly irregular: je vais · tu vas · il va · nous allons · vous allez · ils vont.
**au supermarché** — **à + le = au** (mandatory contraction).
**Aller** also forms the near future: je vais + infinitive = I'm going to…

**chez moi** = at my place / to my place. **chez** is always followed by a person (or pronoun), never a place name: **chez moi** · **chez toi** · **chez le médecin** · **chez Paul**.
**Viens** is the **tu** imperative of **venir** (irregular).

**adorer + infinitive** = to love doing something: j'adore voyager · elle adore lire.
**Voyager** has a spelling change to preserve the soft G sound before **-ons**: nous voyageons (not *nous voyagons*).

**jusqu'au travail** — **jusqu'à + le = jusqu'au** (mandatory contraction with **jusqu'à**).
**marcher** = to walk (as locomotion); **se promener** = to stroll/go for a walk (leisure). **marcher** also means 'to work/function': ça marche ? (does it work?).
cards.englishPhrase: I walk to work every day.
cards.phrase: Je marche jusqu'au travail tous les jours.

cards.grammarNote:
**jusqu'au bureau** — **jusqu'à + le = jusqu'au**.
**conduire** is irregular: je conduis · tu conduis · il conduit · nous conduisons · vous conduisez · ils conduisent.

**Tournez** is the **vous** imperative of the regular -er verb **tourner**.
**à gauche** (left) · **à droite** (right) · **au coin** (**à + le** = au — mandatory contraction).

**Traversez** is the **vous** imperative of the regular -er verb **traverser**.
**avec précaution** = carefully (lit. with caution). **Précaution** is cognate with English 'precaution'.

**suivre** is irregular: je suis · tu suis · il suit · nous suivons · vous suivez · ils suivent.
Warning: **je suis** = I follow AND I am (**être**) — context distinguishes them.

**entrer par** = to enter through/by (a means of entry).
**Entrez** is the **vous** imperative. **Entrer** uses **être** in the passé composé: je suis entré(e) (I entered).

**partir de** = to leave from: je pars **du** travail (**de + le = du** — mandatory contraction).
**partir** is irregular: je pars · tu pars · il part · nous partons · vous partez · ils partent.
cards.phrase: Je pars du travail à cinq heures.

cards.grammarNote:
**arriver** uses **être** in the passé composé: on est arrivé(e)s.
**demain** = tomorrow — adverbs of time go after the conjugated verb or at the start/end of the sentence: on arrive **demain** · **demain**, on arrive.

**visiter** is used for places: visiter le musée, visiter Paris.
To visit a person, use **rendre visite à**: je rends visite à ma grand-mère (I'm visiting my grandmother). Never use **visiter** for people.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to visit the museum.

cards.grammarNote:
**près du centre-ville** — **près de + le = près du** (**de + le = du** — mandatory contraction).
**habiter** can be used with or without a preposition: j'habite Paris · j'habite **à** Paris · j'habite **dans** un appartement — all correct, slight differences in register.
cards.englishPhrase: I live near the city centre.

cards.grammarNote:
**séjourner** (used in the phrase) = to stay (at a hotel/for a period of time); **rester** = to stay/remain (in place or state).
**dans un hôtel** — **dans** (inside a specific place).

**je t'attends** — **t'** is the **tu** direct object pronoun (elided before a vowel): je t'attends = I'm waiting for you.
**attendre** takes a direct object in French: j'attends **le** bus (I'm waiting for the bus) — no **pour** needed, unlike English.

**au parc** — **à + le = au** (mandatory contraction).
**se retrouver** = to meet up (by prior arrangement): on se retrouve au parc.
**rencontrer** = to meet (for the first time or by chance): on s'est rencontrés à l'université.

**se perdre** is reflexive: je me perds · tu te perds · il se perd
Many movement verbs are reflexive: **se promener** (to stroll), **se diriger** (to head toward), **s'en aller** (to leave).

**je ne trouve pas** — negation wraps the verb: **ne** … **pas**. Before a vowel, **ne** stays: je **ne** trouve **pas**.
**trouver** = to find (physically) or to find/think (opinion): je trouve ça difficile (I find that difficult).

**chercher** takes a direct object — no preposition needed: je cherche **la** pharmacie (not *je cherche pour la pharmacie*).
Contrast English 'look for' (two words) vs. French **chercher** (one verb, no preposition).

**s'arrêter** is reflexive: je m'arrête · tu t'arrêtes · il s'arrête.
**Arrêtez-vous** = reflexive imperative (**vous** form): the reflexive pronoun **vous** follows the verb with a hyphen.

**se garer** is reflexive: je me gare · tu te gares · il se gare.
**où est-ce que je peux** — **pouvoir + infinitive** = to be able to. **est-ce que** is the question marker that avoids inversion in informal/spoken French.
cards.phrase: Où est-ce que je peux me garer ?

cards.grammarNote:
**animé(e)** = lively/busy/crowded (lit. animated). It agrees in gender: **animé** (masc.) · **animée** (fem.): un quartier animé · une rue animée.
**Le marché** = the market (masculine). **Marché** appears in **supermarché** (supermarket).

**calme** does not change for masculine/feminine: un quartier **calme** · une rue **calme** (invariable adjective ending in **-e**).
**je préfère** — **préférer** has an accent change: je **préfère** · nous **préférons** (the accent goes from é to è before a silent syllable).

**perdu(e)** — past participle of **perdre**, used as an adjective. It agrees with the subject: je suis **perdu** (m.) · je suis **perdue** (f.).
**Je suis perdu(e)** uses **être** (state). Compare the reflexive verb: je me suis **perdu** (I got lost — in the passé composé).

cards.english: I am a doctor. (no article: je suis médecin)
cards.grammarNote:
State a job with **être** and **no article**:
**je suis médecin** (I'm a doctor), **elle est ingénieure** (she's an engineer). Add an article only with a description: **c'est un bon médecin**.

To say you like doing something, use **aimer** + the infinitive:
**j'aime lire** (I like reading), **j'aime courir** (I like running). No 'to' or '-ing' — just the plain verb.

After **être**, omit the article with professions: Je suis médecin (not *un médecin*).
Add the article only when the noun is modified: Je suis **un** bon médecin.
This applies to all professions: Elle est avocate · Il est ingénieur.

**infirmier** (masc.) → **infirmière** (fem.) — a gendered profession noun.
After **être**, no article: elle est **infirmière** (not *une infirmière*).
**chez l'infirmier / chez l'infirmière** = at the nurse's (office).

Traditionally masculine, **ingénieur** is now also used as **ingénieure** (fem.) in modern French.
After **être**: mon frère est **ingénieur** — no article unless modified: c'est **un** ingénieur **brillant**.

**comme** = as/like: je travaille **comme** développeur (I work as a developer).
**programmeur** (masc.) · **programmeuse** (fem.); **développeur** (masc.) · **développeuse** (fem.) — the phrase uses **développeur** as the more common tech-industry term.

**cuisinier** (masc.) → **cuisinière** (fem.).
**en cuisine** = in the kitchen (professional context, no article — fixed expression). Compare: **dans la cuisine** = in the kitchen (of a home).
cards.englishPhrase: The cook works in the kitchen.

cards.grammarNote:
**serveur** (masc.) → **serveuse** (fem.) — a gendered noun pair.
**a apporté** — passé composé with **avoir**: il a + apporté (past participle of **apporter**, a regular -er verb).
**la carte** = the menu (in a restaurant). Do not confuse with **la carte** (map/card).
cards.phrase: Le serveur a apporté la carte.

cards.grammarNote:
**directeur** (masc.) → **directrice** (fem.) — note the **-trice** feminine ending.
After **être**: elle est **directrice** — no article. With modification: c'est **une** directrice **efficace**.

**étudiant(e)** — masculine **étudiant** · feminine **étudiante**.
After **être**: je suis **étudiant(e)** — no article. This rule applies to all professions and social roles.
**L'étudiant** starts with a vowel — elision: l'étudiant, l'étudiante.

**architecte** is the same for masculine and feminine: il est **architecte** · elle est **architecte**.
After **être**: il est **architecte** — no article. It is an epicene (gender-invariant) profession noun.

**avocat** (masc.) → **avocate** (fem.).
After **être**: ma sœur est **avocate** — no article.
Also means 'avocado' (**l'avocat**) — a famous French false amis within French itself!

**Quel est le salaire ?** — **quel** is the masculine interrogative adjective agreeing with **salaire** (masc.).
**Le salaire** = salary/wage. Related: **le smic** = minimum wage · **une augmentation de salaire** = a pay rise.

**l'emploi du temps** — **du** = **de + le** (mandatory contraction): l'emploi **du** temps (lit. the use of time).
**flexible** is an invariable adjective (same for masc. and fem.): un horaire **flexible** · une organisation **flexible**.
cards.phrase: Mon emploi du temps est flexible.

cards.grammarNote:
**en vacances** = on vacation (fixed expression with **en**, no article).
**les vacances** is always plural in French — there is no singular form in common use.
**la semaine prochaine** = next week. Time expressions: la semaine **prochaine** · le mois **prochain** · l'année **prochaine**.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going on vacation next week.
cards.phrase: Je pars en vacances la semaine prochaine.

cards.grammarNote:
**Prenons une pause** — **prenons** is the **nous** imperative of **prendre** (irregular).
**faire une pause** is also very common: faisons **une pause**. **La pause** = break/pause (cognate with English).
**dans un bureau** — **dans** (inside a space). **Le bureau** = office AND desk — context distinguishes: je travaille **au bureau** (at the office) vs. le livre est sur **le bureau** (on the desk).

**mes collègues** — **mes** is the plural possessive adjective for all genders.
**sympas** is the informal/abbreviated form of **sympathiques** (friendly/nice). It is invariable in this informal form: ils sont **sympas** · elles sont **sympas**.

**client** (masc.) → **cliente** (fem.).
**content** (masc.) → **contente** (fem.): le client est **content** · la cliente est **contente**.
**Le client** = client/customer. **Le consommateur** = consumer (broader term).

**dans une super équipe** — **dans** (inside a group/context).
**super** is an invariable informal adjective: une **super** équipe · un **super** travail — it never changes form.
cards.englishPhrase: I work in a great team.
cards.phrase: Je travaille dans une super équipe.

cards.grammarNote:
**presque terminé** — **presque** = almost/nearly (adverb, invariable).
**terminé** is the past participle of **terminer** used as an adjective: le projet est presque **terminé** (masc.) · la tâche est presque **terminée** (fem.).

**à dix heures** — time expressions use **à**: à huit heures · à dix heures · à midi.
**on a une réunion** — **on** used colloquially for 'we'. **avoir** + noun = to have something: on **a** une réunion.
cards.englishPhrase: We have a meeting at ten.
cards.phrase: On a une réunion à dix heures.

cards.grammarNote:
**pendant ton temps libre** — **pendant** = during. **ton** = your (masc. sing. informal).
**Qu'est-ce que tu fais** — inversion-free question structure: **qu'est-ce que** + subject + verb. **fais** = second-person singular of **faire** (irregular).
cards.englishPhrase: What do you do in your free time?
cards.phrase: Qu'est-ce que tu fais pendant ton temps libre ?

cards.english: I work as a nurse. (travailler comme / dans / chez)
cards.grammarNote:
**travailler comme** = to work as; **travailler dans** = in (a field/place); **travailler chez** = at (a company):
**je travaille comme infirmier**, **dans un hôpital**, **chez Google**.

**travailler dans** = to work in (a specific place): je travaille **dans** un hôpital.
**travailler comme** = to work as: je travaille **comme** médecin.
**un hôpital** — masculine noun starting with H aspirate, so no elision or liaison: **un** hôpital, **le** hôpital → actually **l'hôpital** (the H here is mute/aspirate — learners should check each H word).

**aimer + infinitive** = to like doing: j'aime **lire**.
**lire** is irregular: je lis · tu lis · il lit · nous lisons · vous lisez · ils lisent.
The hobby noun is **la lecture** (reading as an activity): la lecture est mon passe-temps préféré.

**écrire** is irregular: j'écris · tu écris · il écrit · nous écrivons · vous écrivez · ils écrivent.
**des histoires** — **de + les = des** (mandatory contraction); also the indefinite plural article: elle écrit **des** histoires.

**peindre** is irregular: je peins · tu peins · il peint · nous peignons · vous peignez · ils peignent.
**adorer + infinitive** = to love doing: il adore **peindre**. **Adorer** is stronger than **aimer**.

**dessiner** is a regular **-er** verb: je dessine · tu dessines · il dessine.
The noun: **le dessin** (a drawing / the art of drawing). **un dessinateur / une dessinatrice** = an illustrator/draughtsman.

**de la musique** — after **écouter**, the partitive article is used: j'écoute **de la** musique (some music).
**faire de la musique** = to make/play music: **faire de la** (fem.) · **faire du** (masc.) · **faire de l'** (vowel): faire **du** sport · faire **de la** randonnée.
cards.englishPhrase: I listen to music every day.
cards.phrase: J'écoute de la musique tous les jours.

cards.grammarNote:
**chanter** is a regular **-er** verb: je chante · tu chantes · il chante.
**adorer + infinitive**: elle adore **chanter**. The noun for singing: **le chant** (singing/song as an art form).

**jouer de** = to play an instrument: jouer du piano · jouer de la guitare · jouer du violon
**jouer à** = to play a sport or game: jouer au foot · jouer aux échecs

**danser** is a regular **-er** verb: je danse · tu danses · il danse.
**On adore danser** — **on** used colloquially for 'we'. The noun: **la danse** (dancing). **faire de la danse** is also used for dance as a hobby.

**cuisiner** is a regular **-er** verb: je cuisine · tu cuisines · il cuisine.
**faire de la cuisine** is an alternative: j'aime **faire de la cuisine**. The noun: **la cuisine** = cooking AND kitchen.

**faire de la randonnée** — **faire + de la** because **randonnée** is feminine.
**en montagne** = in the mountains (fixed expression, no article). Compare: **dans la montagne** (in/through a specific mountain).
cards.englishPhrase: I like hiking in the mountains.
cards.phrase: J'aime faire de la randonnée en montagne.

cards.grammarNote:
**courir** is irregular: je cours · tu cours · il court · nous courons · vous courez · ils courent.
**tous les matins** = every morning. **Tous** (all/every, masc. pl.) · **toutes** (fem. pl.): tous les jours · toutes les semaines.

cards.english: I go swimming. (faire de la natation)
cards.grammarNote:
Many sports and hobbies use **faire de** + activity:
**je fais de la natation** (I swim), **je fais du vélo** (I cycle). **faire** is irregular: **je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font**.
cards.englishPhrase: I go hiking on the weekend.
cards.phrase: Je fais de la randonnée le week-end.

cards.grammarNote:
**nager** has a spelling change to keep the soft G before **-ons**: nous **nageons** (not *nous nagons*).
As a sport: **faire de la natation** (to swim as a sport). **Nager** = the act of swimming; **la natation** = swimming as a discipline.

**faire du vélo** — **faire + du** because **vélo** is masculine (**de + le = du** — mandatory contraction).
Same pattern: **faire du sport** · **faire du yoga** · **faire du ski** · **faire de la natation** (swimming, fem.).
cards.phrase: Je fais du vélo le week-end.

cards.grammarNote:
**voyager** has a spelling change before **-ons**: nous **voyageons** (the E preserves the soft G sound).
**j'adore voyager** — **adorer + infinitive** = to love doing something. Compare: **j'aime voyager** (I like travelling).

**jouer aux jeux vidéo** — **jouer à + les = jouer aux** (**à + les = aux** — mandatory contraction).
**le soir** = in the evening (no preposition 'in' — just the definite article **le**).
cards.englishPhrase: He plays video games at night.
cards.phrase: Il joue aux jeux vidéo le soir.

cards.grammarNote:
**regarder des films** — **des** is the indefinite plural article (**de + les = des** — mandatory contraction).
**aimer + infinitive**: j'aime **regarder**. **Regarder** = to watch/look at (directed attention); **voir** = to see (perception).

**écouter de la musique** — **de la** is the partitive article (some music), used after **écouter**.
**aimer + infinitive**: elle aime **écouter**. **Écouter** = to listen to (no separate preposition 'to' needed: j'écoute **la** radio).
cards.phrase: Elle aime écouter de la musique.

cards.grammarNote:
**à la salle de sport** — **à + la** (feminine noun, no contraction).
**faire de l'exercice** — **faire + de l'** because **exercice** starts with a vowel (**de + l' = de l'**, no contraction).
cards.englishPhrase: I go to the gym for exercise.
cards.phrase: Je vais à la salle de sport pour faire de l'exercice.

cards.grammarNote:
**en plein air** = outdoors / in the open air. **En** is used without an article in this fixed expression.
Compare: **à l'extérieur** (outside/outdoors, more formal) · **dehors** (outside, as an adverb: il fait froid **dehors**).

**créatif** (masc.) → **créative** (fem.): elle est très **créative**.
Adjectives ending in **-if** change to **-ive** in the feminine: créatif/créative · actif/active · sportif/sportive.

**intéressant** (masc.) → **intéressante** (fem.): une réunion **intéressante**.
**mon travail** — possessive adjective: **mon** (masc. sing.) · **ma** (fem. sing.) · **mes** (plural). Before vowels: **mon** is used even for feminine nouns: **mon** amie.

**ennuyeux** (masc.) → **ennuyeuse** (fem.): la réunion était **ennuyeuse**.
Adjectives ending in **-eux** change to **-euse** in the feminine: ennuyeux/ennuyeuse · heureux/heureuse · sérieux/sérieuse.

**gagner** = to earn / to win. **Il gagne un bon salaire** = he earns a good salary.
**bon** = good (masculine); **bonne** (feminine): un **bon** salaire · une **bonne** idée. **Bon** precedes the noun it modifies.

**prendre sa retraite** = to retire (lit. to take one's retirement). This is a fixed expression.
**a pris** — passé composé of **prendre** (irregular): past participle **pris**. Elle **a pris** sa retraite l'année dernière.
cards.phrase: Elle a pris sa retraite l'année dernière.

cards.grammarNote:
**avoir un travail** = to have a job. **Le travail** (masc.) = work/job. Irregular plural: **les travaux** (works/tasks/roadworks).
**un bon travail** — **bon** precedes masculine nouns: **un bon** travail · **une bonne** situation.

**au chômage** — **à + le = au** (mandatory contraction). **être au chômage** is a fixed expression for 'to be unemployed'.
**en ce moment** = currently / at the moment. A common time adverbial: il est **en ce moment** au chômage.
cards.phrase: Il est au chômage en ce moment.

cards.grammarNote:
**étudier** is a regular **-er** verb: j'étudie · tu étudies · il étudie · nous étudions · vous étudiez · ils étudient.
**tous les jours** = every day: **tous** (masc. pl.) + **les** + noun.

**apprendre** is irregular (like **prendre**): j'apprends · tu apprends · il apprend · nous apprenons · vous apprenez · ils apprennent.
**le français** — language names take the definite article when used as objects: j'apprends **le** français · elle parle **l'**espagnol.

**pratiquer** is a regular **-er** verb: je pratique · tu pratiques · il pratique.
Also common: **s'entraîner** (to train/practise, reflexive) · **faire des exercices** (to do exercises).

**enseigner** is a regular **-er** verb: elle enseigne · nous enseignons.
